Exposure associations in single-cell data with exposomeSC

Cuiwei Gao

26 November 2026

Source: vignettes/exposomeSC.Rmd
exposomeSC.Rmd

Abstract

exposomeSC relates exposures measured on donors to gene expression within the annotated cell types of single-cell RNA-seq data. This vignette goes through the package on two small real data sets: airway epithelial cells of smokers and never smokers from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, and blood cells of patients whose plasma was measured for compounds of exogenous origin. It covers the container, the donor-pseudobulk association model and its companions, and the analyses built around it.

Introduction

exposomeSC relates exposures measured on donors to gene expression within the annotated cell types of single-cell RNA-seq data. Its container, the SingleCellExposomeExperiment, keeps a donor-level exposure table next to the cells of a SingleCellExperiment and checks that the two agree. Its main analysis, run_sc_exwas(), sums the raw counts of each cell type within each donor and fits a model in which the donors, not the cells, are the replicates.

Cells of one donor share that donor’s exposure, so they are not independent observations of it; a test that treats them as such is too confident (Squair et al. 2021). The quantity that run_sc_exwas() estimates is the log2 fold change of a gene’s expression rate within a cell type per unit of the exposure. A change in the number of cells of a type is a different quantity and has a function of its own (Section @ref(composition)).

The package works with the classes of Bioconductor. The container extends SingleCellExperiment, the pseudobulk counts are SummarizedExperiment objects, and the results are DataFrames; those of run_sc_exwas() carry the settings of the run in their metadata(). The models are fitted by edgeR, DESeq2 and limma. In a workflow the package comes after quality control and the annotation of cell types, which it takes as given: its input is a SingleCellExperiment with raw counts, a column that names the donor of each cell and a column with the cell type.

Every association the package estimates is observational. Exposures such as smoking are not assigned at random, and nothing in the package identifies a causal effect.

The vignette uses the two data sets that the package ships. Both are real and both are small on purpose: they show what the functions take and what they return, and they are far too small to support conclusions. The first, 352 airway epithelial cells of 12 donors, serves Sections @ref(data) to @ref(composition). The second, 1,032 blood cells of 43 patients with measured plasma compounds and surface proteins, serves Section @ref(incov).

Some sections use packages that exposomeSC only suggests: lme4, lmerTest and pbkrtest, mgcv, qgcomp, metafor, ppcor, variancePartition and fgsea. A chunk that needs one of them is run when it is installed. Two further vignettes cover the cross-omic networks and checks of a result by permutation.

Installation 

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("exposomeSC")

The airway data 

library(exposomeSC)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
x <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "hlca_airway_subset.rds",
    package = "exposomeSC"))
x
#> class: SingleCellExposomeExperiment 
#> dim: 20111 352 
#> metadata(1): source
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(20111): ENSG00000000003 ENSG00000000419 ... ENSG00000283103
#>   ENSG00000283125
#> rowData names(1): symbol
#> colnames(352): TCTTCCTTCAGAGCAG_T101 CTACTATCAACGGGTA_T101 ...
#>   CCTCTAGAGCAAGCCA_T90 CCTCATGGTCTACATG_T90
#> colData names(4): donor_id cell_type assay hlca_donor_id
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(0):
#> exposureData(12 samples x 4 exposures): smoking, chemistry_v3, age, sex_male
#> sampleColumn: donor_id

The object holds the raw counts of 352 tracheal epithelial cells of the Human Lung Cell Atlas core (Sikkema et al. 2023), from its study of smokers and never smokers (Goldfarbmuren et al. 2020): six heavy smokers, with at least 15 pack-years, and six never smokers, with up to 10 basal, 10 secretory and 10 multiciliated-lineage cells per donor. ?hlca_airway_subset describes the selection, and the script that made the file from the public H5AD is installed with the package (system.file("scripts", package = "exposomeSC")). The atlas is distributed under the CC BY 4.0 licence, and the object carries its provenance:

metadata(x)$source[c("data", "dataset_version", "licence", "references")]
#> $data
#> [1] "Human Lung Cell Atlas (HLCA) core, study Seibold_2020"
#> 
#> $dataset_version
#> [1] "688185ad-11c2-4172-a53a-f4f1f4076860"
#> 
#> $licence
#> [1] "CC BY 4.0"
#> 
#> $references
#> [1] "doi:10.1038/s41591-023-02327-2" "doi:10.1038/s41467-020-16239-z"
table(x$donor_id, x$cell_type)
#>       
#>        Basal Multiciliated lineage Secretory
#>   T101    10                    10        10
#>   T120    10                    10        10
#>   T126    10                    10        10
#>   T137    10                    10        10
#>   T153    10                    10        10
#>   T154    10                     2        10
#>   T164    10                    10        10
#>   T165    10                    10        10

#>   T90     10                    10        10

The donor-level variables are the exposure data of the object, one row per donor, with a description of each variable. sampleColumn() names the column of colData() that assigns the cells to the donors.

exposureData(x)
#>      smoking chemistry_v3 age sex_male
#> T101       1            1  55        1
#> T120       1            0  57        0
#> T126       0            0  35        0
#> T137       0            0  27        0
#> T153       0            1  38        1
#> T154       1            1  61        1
#> T164       0            1  66        1
#> T165       0            1  64        1
#> T166       0            1  68        0
#> T167       1            1  66        0
#> T85        1            0  59        1
#> T90        1            1  44        1
exposureInfo(x)
#> DataFrame with 4 rows and 3 columns
#>       exposure        family                   unit
#>    <character>   <character>            <character>
#> 1      smoking tobacco smoke 1 = heavy smoker, 0 ..
#> 2 chemistry_v3     technical 1 = 10x 3' v3, 0 = 1..
#> 3          age   demographic                  years
#> 4     sex_male   demographic   1 = male, 0 = female
exposureVariables(x)
#> [1] "smoking"      "chemistry_v3" "age"          "sex_male"
sampleColumn(x)
#> [1] "donor_id"
head(cellSampleMap(x), 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 2 columns
#>                 cell_id   sample_id
#>             <character> <character>
#> 1 TCTTCCTTCAGAGCAG_T101        T101
#> 2 CTACTATCAACGGGTA_T101        T101
#> 3 ACAAGCTGTGCTGCAC_T101        T101

build_scee() makes such an object from a SingleCellExperiment and a numeric matrix with one row per donor. It stops when a donor of the cells has no row in the matrix or a row has no cells. Here the object is taken apart and built again:

sce <- SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = counts(x)),
    colData = colData(x),
    rowData = rowData(x)
)
rebuilt <- build_scee(sce, exposureData(x), sample_col = "donor_id",
    exposure_info = exposureInfo(x))
identical(exposureData(rebuilt), exposureData(x))
#> [1] TRUE

Donor variables often arrive as columns of the cell annotations, with the value of a donor repeated for each of its cells, as in the metadata of a Seurat object. seurat_to_exposure() reduces such columns to the matrix that build_scee() takes:

cell_table <- data.frame(donor_id = x$donor_id,
    exposureData(x)[x$donor_id, ], row.names = colnames(x))
head(cell_table, 3)
#>                       donor_id smoking chemistry_v3 age sex_male
#> TCTTCCTTCAGAGCAG_T101     T101       1            1  55        1
#> CTACTATCAACGGGTA_T101     T101       1            1  55        1
#> ACAAGCTGTGCTGCAC_T101     T101       1            1  55        1
donor_table <- seurat_to_exposure(cell_table, sample_col = "donor_id",
    exposure_cols = exposureVariables(x))
identical(donor_table, exposureData(x))
#> [1] TRUE

donor_pseudobulk() returns the counts that run_sc_exwas() fits its models to: one SummarizedExperiment per cell type, with one column per donor and the exposure data as column data. Looking at them is the first check of any result. The counts of CYP1B1 in basal cells, a gene that returns below, are:

pseudobulk <- donor_pseudobulk(x)
pseudobulk
#> List of length 3
#> names(3): Basal Multiciliated lineage Secretory
basal <- pseudobulk[["Basal"]]
cyp1b1 <- rownames(x)[rowData(x)$symbol == "CYP1B1"]
data.frame(
    smoking = basal$smoking,
    CYP1B1 = assay(basal, "counts")[cyp1b1, ],
    all_genes = colSums(assay(basal, "counts"))
)
#>      smoking CYP1B1 all_genes
#> T101       1      3    361506
#> T120       1     10    205282
#> T126       0      0    148021
#> T137       0      0    189713
#> T153       0      0    250864
#> T154       1     18    465165
#> T164       0      0    352726
#> T165       0      0    422411
#> T166       0      0    362814
#> T167       1     12    450820
#> T85        1      1    130760
#> T90        1      5    299829

The association model

run_sc_exwas() fits, for each cell type, a donor-level model of the pseudobulk counts on the exposure and the covariates. The default backend is the quasi-likelihood model of edgeR (Chen et al. 2025). Here the exposure is smoking, adjusted for the 10x chemistry, which differs between donors:

fit <- run_sc_exwas(x, exposure = "smoking", covariates = "chemistry_v3")
dim(fit)
#> [1] 32890    17
top <- head(fit, 8)
top$symbol <- rowData(x)[top$gene, "symbol"]
top[, c("symbol", "celltype", "log2FC", "statistic", "pvalue", "padj",
    "padj_global", "n_donors")]
#> DataFrame with 8 rows and 8 columns
#>        symbol              celltype    log2FC statistic      pvalue       padj
#>   <character>           <character> <numeric> <numeric>   <numeric>  <numeric>
#> 1       IL1R2                 Basal   2.96110   6.37915 5.17735e-07 0.00554391
#> 2        LDLR Multiciliated lineage   1.33962   6.01446 1.52521e-06 0.01105868
#> 3        KILH Multiciliated lineage   2.30558   5.79025 1.98558e-06 0.01105868
#> 4      CYP1B1                 Basal   5.97497   6.43537 2.86266e-06 0.01532670
#> 5      MIPOL1 Multiciliated lineage   2.05317   5.50351 5.04406e-06 0.01872859
#> 6        SAA4             Secretory  -3.46544  -5.41085 8.61588e-06 0.09514516
#> 7        PSCA Multiciliated lineage   1.32515   5.32518 1.02146e-05 0.02844509
#> 8      FGFBP1 Multiciliated lineage   2.81946   5.75107 1.33446e-05 0.02861956
#>   padj_global  n_donors
#>     <numeric> <integer>
#> 1   0.0170283        12
#> 2   0.0217686        11
#> 3   0.0217686        11
#> 4   0.0235382        12
#> 5   0.0331798        11
#> 6   0.0472294        12
#> 7   0.0479940        11
#> 8   0.0548628        11

The result has one row per tested gene and cell type, ordered by padj_global. padj is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment within a cell type and padj_global the adjustment across all tested gene-by-cell-type pairs. For the edgeR backend se is NA: the quasi-likelihood F test gives no standard error of the coefficient, and statistic is the square root of the F statistic with the sign of the log fold change. The settings and what was done in each cell type are kept with the result:

parameters <- metadata(fit)$parameters
parameters[c("method", "se_method", "statistic_type")]
#> $method
#> [1] "edgeR"
#> 
#> $se_method
#> [1] "not_available_edgeR_QL"
#> 
#> $statistic_type
#> [1] "signed_sqrt_qlf"
diagnostics <- metadata(fit)$diagnostics
vapply(diagnostics, function(d) d$n_donors, numeric(1))
#>                 Basal Multiciliated lineage             Secretory 
#>                    12                    11                    12
vapply(diagnostics, function(d) d$n_genes_tested, numeric(1))
#>                 Basal Multiciliated lineage             Secretory 
#>                 10708                 11139                 11043

One donor has only two multiciliated-lineage cells, fewer than min_cells, so that cell type is fitted with 11 donors.

These numbers must not be read as findings. With six donors per group and at most ten cells per donor and cell type, a few counts decide a result: the table of Section @ref(data) shows that CYP1B1 has no count in the basal cells of the never smokers and between 1 and 18 in those of a smoker, and the size of such an estimate depends on little. The same model on larger sets of cells of the same donors, which were analysed when the data set was made, gave other lists of genes below a threshold.

Other models for the same question

Other backends

method = "voom_dream" fits the voom model of limma through variancePartition (Hoffman and Roussos 2021), and method = "DESeq2" a Wald test of DESeq2. Both return a standard error of the coefficient. The columns are the same for every backend.

fit_voom <- run_sc_exwas(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", method = "voom_dream", celltypes = "Basal")
fit_voom$symbol <- rowData(x)[fit_voom$gene, "symbol"]
head(fit_voom[, c("symbol", "log2FC", "se", "statistic", "pvalue")], 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 5 columns
#>        symbol    log2FC        se statistic      pvalue
#>   <character> <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>   <numeric>
#> 1      CYP1B1   3.76235  0.477184   7.88450 3.54114e-08
#> 2       IL1R2   2.63220  0.472469   5.57117 9.20432e-06
#> 3         NTS  -1.40107  0.276195  -5.07276 3.26980e-05

A negative binomial model with an offset

run_sc_exwas_pb_offset() fits a negative binomial model of each pseudobulk count with the logarithm of the donor’s total count as offset (Lee and Han 2024), for the genes named in target_genes, here three. Its p-values are Wald tests and can be too small with few donors. It has no padj within a cell type; padj_global is adjusted across the tests that were made. It also has no min_cells: every donor with a cell of the type enters the model, the donor with two multiciliated-lineage cells included.

genes <- rownames(x)[match(c("ALDH3A1", "NQO1", "GPX2"), rowData(x)$symbol)]
offset_fit <- run_sc_exwas_pb_offset(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", target_genes = genes)
offset_fit$symbol <- rowData(x)[offset_fit$gene, "symbol"]
offset_fit[, c("symbol", "celltype", "log2FC", "se", "statistic", "pvalue",
    "padj_global")]
#> DataFrame with 9 rows and 7 columns
#>        symbol              celltype     log2FC        se statistic      pvalue
#>   <character>           <character>  <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>   <numeric>
#> 1     ALDH3A1 Multiciliated lineage  1.6639367  0.477171  3.487085 0.000488316
#> 2        GPX2 Multiciliated lineage  0.9285628  0.288305  3.220771 0.001278462
#> 3        NQO1 Multiciliated lineage  0.5981829  0.255481  2.341396 0.019211799

#> 5        GPX2                 Basal -0.3673234  0.272701 -1.346983 0.177985593
#> 6     ALDH3A1             Secretory  0.5849155  0.676691  0.864376 0.387381420
#> 7        NQO1                 Basal -0.1472037  0.349979 -0.420607 0.674042118
#> 8        NQO1             Secretory  0.0879069  0.474085  0.185424 0.852896333
#> 9     ALDH3A1                 Basal  0.0800406  0.459262  0.174281 0.861644575
#>   padj_global
#>     <numeric>
#> 1  0.00439485
#> 2  0.00575308
#> 3  0.05763540
#> 4  0.25896415
#> 5  0.32037407
#> 6  0.58107213
#> 7  0.86164458
#> 8  0.86164458
#> 9  0.86164458

A mixed model of the cells

run_sc_exwas_glmm() keeps the cells as observations. For each gene it fits a linear mixed model of the log-normalised expression of the cells, with random intercepts for the donor and for the donor within a cell type, and tests the effect of the exposure in each cell type with denominator degrees of freedom by the method of Satterthwaite, the default, or of Kenward and Roger, which its help page advises for fewer than about 30 donors and which is used here. It is much slower than the pseudobulk models, so it is meant for a few genes.

mixed_fit <- run_sc_exwas_glmm(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", target_genes = genes,
    ddf = "Kenward-Roger")
mixed_fit$symbol <- rowData(x)[mixed_fit$gene, "symbol"]
mixed_fit[, c("symbol", "celltype", "log2FC", "se", "df", "pvalue",
    "padj_global")]
#> DataFrame with 9 rows and 7 columns
#>        symbol              celltype     log2FC        se        df    pvalue
#>   <character>           <character>  <numeric> <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>
#> 1     ALDH3A1 Multiciliated lineage  1.1937568  0.522799   13.4336 0.0392683
#> 2        NQO1 Multiciliated lineage  0.3922636  0.229207   23.1645 0.1003672
#> 3        GPX2 Multiciliated lineage  0.4269340  0.262276   17.3609 0.1215772
#> 4        GPX2                 Basal -0.3678811  0.256765   16.3480 0.1707738
#> 5        GPX2             Secretory  0.2085547  0.256765   16.3480 0.4283237
#> 6     ALDH3A1             Secretory  0.3727827  0.516562   12.9032 0.4833755
#> 7        NQO1                 Basal -0.1391103  0.223053   21.8187 0.5393143
#> 8     ALDH3A1                 Basal -0.1347923  0.516562   12.9032 0.7982561
#> 9        NQO1             Secretory  0.0514866  0.223053   21.8187 0.8196001
#>   padj_global
#>     <numeric>
#> 1    0.353415
#> 2    0.364732
#> 3    0.364732
#> 4    0.384241
#> 5    0.693404
#> 6    0.693404
#> 7    0.693404
#> 8    0.819600
#> 9    0.819600

The response is log2(counts per 10,000 + 1) of each cell, so the coefficient, although the column is called log2FC, is not on the scale of the pseudobulk estimates. family = "nbinom" fits a negative binomial mixed model with a likelihood-ratio test for each gene and cell type instead; that takes minutes for a few genes even on these data and is not run here.

More than one exposure, and differences between cell types

run_multi_exwas() runs the model for several exposures and adds padj_all, the adjustment across all exposures and cell types. Age is used here as a second donor variable; celltypes restricts the run to basal cells.

both <- run_multi_exwas(x, exposures = c("smoking", "age"),
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", celltypes = "Basal")
#> Running sc-ExWAS for: smoking
#> Running sc-ExWAS for: age
table(both$exposure)
#> 
#>     age smoking 
#>   10708   10708
both$symbol <- rowData(x)[both$gene, "symbol"]
head(both[, c("symbol", "exposure", "log2FC", "pvalue", "padj_global",
    "padj_all")], 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 6 columns
#>        symbol    exposure    log2FC      pvalue padj_global  padj_all
#>   <character> <character> <numeric>   <numeric>   <numeric> <numeric>
#> 1       IL1R2     smoking   2.96110 5.17735e-07  0.00554391 0.0110878
#> 2      CYP1B1     smoking   5.97497 2.86266e-06  0.01532670 0.0306534
#> 3      TSPAN8     smoking  -2.49851 2.03721e-05  0.05522154 0.1104431

A small p-value in one cell type and a large one in another do not show that the effect differs between the two (Gelman and Stern 2006). run_interaction_test() tests the difference itself, for the genes in target_genes or, by default, for the 50 most variable genes:

interaction <- run_interaction_test(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3")
interaction$symbol <- rowData(x)[interaction$gene, "symbol"]
head(interaction[order(interaction$p_interaction),
    c("symbol", "p_interaction", "padj_interaction", "n_celltypes",
        "n_donors")], 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 5 columns
#>        symbol p_interaction padj_interaction n_celltypes  n_donors
#>   <character>     <numeric>        <numeric>   <integer> <integer>
#> 1      BPIFA1     0.0142263         0.711314           3        12
#> 2       WDR38     0.0675888         0.957566           3        12
#> 3     DYNLRB2     0.0972912         0.957566           3        12

Gene sets

run_gsea() ranks the genes of each cell type by the test statistic and runs fgsea on the ranking. Gene sets are named lists of gene identifiers as in the row names of the object. The three sets below are short lists written for this example, not a curated collection; they are mapped from symbols to the Ensembl identifiers of the data.

symbols <- list(
    xenobiotic_response = c("CYP1B1", "CYP1A1", "AHRR", "ALDH3A1", "NQO1",
        "AKR1C1", "AKR1C2", "AKR1B10", "GPX2", "TXNRD1", "CBR1", "UGT1A6"),
    cilia = c("FOXJ1", "DNAH5", "DNAI1", "CCDC39", "CCDC40", "RSPH1",
        "TEKT1", "DNAH9", "CFAP43", "SPAG6"),
    secretory = c("MUC5AC", "MUC5B", "SCGB1A1", "TFF3", "BPIFB1", "AGR2",
        "SPDEF", "FOXA3")
)
gene_sets <- lapply(symbols, function(set) {
    rownames(x)[rowData(x)$symbol %in% set]
})
lengths(gene_sets)
#> xenobiotic_response               cilia           secretory 
#>                  12                   9                   8
set.seed(1)
enrichment <- run_gsea(fit, gene_sets = gene_sets, min_size = 5L)
enrichment[, c("pathway", "celltype", "NES", "pval", "padj_global", "size")]
#> DataFrame with 7 rows and 6 columns
#>               pathway              celltype       NES        pval padj_global
#>           <character>           <character> <numeric>   <numeric>   <numeric>
#> 1           secretory                 Basal -0.827794 0.697318008  0.69731801
#> 2 xenobiotic_response                 Basal  1.158095 0.284536082  0.33195876
#> 3               cilia Multiciliated lineage -1.564555 0.045194942  0.07909115
#> 4           secretory Multiciliated lineage  1.838749 0.002449421  0.00857297
#> 5 xenobiotic_response Multiciliated lineage  1.927211 0.000589535  0.00412674
#> 6           secretory             Secretory -1.640713 0.021349762  0.04981611
#> 7 xenobiotic_response             Secretory  1.278132 0.173410405  0.24277457
#>        size
#>   <integer>
#> 1         7
#> 2        10
#> 3         9
#> 4         7
#> 5         8
#> 6         8
#> 7         9

size is the number of genes of a set that were tested in the cell type. A set with fewer than min_size of them is left out for that cell type.

Combining cohorts

run_meta_exwas() combines the estimates of independent cohorts by inverse-variance weighting. It needs results with standard errors, so results of the edgeR backend are refused, and its random-effects synthesis (method = "random") needs at least three cohorts. The airway data are one study; to show the function, the four donors measured with the 10x v2 chemistry and the eight measured with v3 are treated as two cohorts, each with too few donors for an analysis of its own, and the genes of the sets above are combined.

v3 <- rownames(exposureData(x))[exposureData(x)[, "chemistry_v3"] == 1]
cohorts <- list(
    v2 = x[, !x$donor_id %in% v3],
    v3 = x[, x$donor_id %in% v3]
)
cohort_fits <- lapply(cohorts, function(cohort) {
    cohort_fit <- run_sc_exwas(cohort, exposure = "smoking",
        method = "voom_dream", celltypes = "Basal", min_donors = 4L)
    cohort_fit[cohort_fit$gene %in% unlist(gene_sets), ]
})
meta <- run_meta_exwas(cohort_fits, cohort_names = names(cohort_fits))
meta$symbol <- rowData(x)[meta$gene, "symbol"]
head(meta[order(meta$meta_pvalue), c("symbol", "meta_effect", "meta_se",
    "meta_pvalue", "n_cohorts", "direction")], 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 6 columns
#>        symbol meta_effect   meta_se meta_pvalue n_cohorts   direction
#>   <character>   <numeric> <numeric>   <numeric> <integer> <character>
#> 1      CYP1B1     3.76661  0.493605 2.33272e-14         2          ++
#> 2     SCGB1A1    -3.01158  0.532967 1.59893e-08         2          --
#> 3      AKR1C1    -1.01850  0.315096 1.22781e-03         2          --

Subsetting the columns of the object keeps the exposure data of the remaining donors. The combination treats the standard error of each cohort as known. With two donors against two in one cohort and four against four in the other they are anything but, so the p-values of this table show how the function is called and nothing about the genes.

Cell composition

run_exposure_composition() asks whether the proportions of the cell types differ with the exposure, with the donors as the units. The cells of the airway data were drawn in equal numbers per donor and cell type, so they carry no information about composition. The provenance record of the object holds the numbers of cells of each donor and cell type in the atlas from which they were drawn, and an object with one label per cell and no counts is enough for the function:

eligible <- metadata(x)$source$eligible_cells
eligible
#>      Basal Multiciliated lineage Secretory
#> T101  2957                   140       112
#> T120  1342                   185       216
#> T126  1454                   192       100
#> T137   911                   282       119
#> T153  2690                   251       394
#> T154  1413                     2       210
#> T164  2913                    79       194
#> T165  1983                    51        33
#> T166  2079                   299       191
#> T167  2220                   163       386
#> T85   3053                   108       316
#> T90   1873                    90       216
cells <- paste0("cell", seq_len(sum(eligible)))
labels <- DataFrame(
    donor_id = rep(rownames(eligible)[row(eligible)], eligible),
    cell_type = rep(colnames(eligible)[col(eligible)], eligible),
    row.names = cells
)
no_counts <- matrix(0, 0, length(cells), dimnames = list(NULL, cells))
atlas_cells <- build_scee(
    SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = no_counts), colData = labels),
    exposureData(x), sample_col = "donor_id"
)
composition <- run_exposure_composition(atlas_cells, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3")
composition[, c("log2_ratio_change", "se", "pvalue", "padj",
    "median_observed_proportion")]
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 5 columns
#>                       log2_ratio_change        se    pvalue      padj
#>                               <numeric> <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>
#> Basal                          0.379082  0.710338  0.606501  0.606501
#> Multiciliated lineage         -1.710891  1.128324  0.163747  0.359128
#> Secretory                      1.331809  0.774701  0.119709  0.359128
#>                       median_observed_proportion
#>                                        <numeric>
#> Basal                                  0.8461646
#> Multiciliated lineage                  0.0512467
#> Secretory                              0.0907921

log2_ratio_change is the coefficient of the exposure for the log2 ratio of a cell type to the geometric mean of the others, with a heteroscedasticity-consistent standard error, and padj is the Holm adjustment over the cell types. A test of the composition as a whole is in metadata(composition)$omnibus. The ratios are among these three cell types as they were captured; they say nothing about absolute numbers of cells in the tissue.

A cohort with measured exposures and proteins

The airway data have a smoking status and no measurement of what the donors were exposed to. The second data set of the package has such measurements: 1,032 blood cells of 43 patients of the INCOV cohort (Su et al. 2020), 14 monocytes and 10 T cells each, with the counts of 192 antibodies for the same cells, four of them isotype controls, and the plasma levels of 13 compounds of exogenous origin among the donor variables. All donors had COVID-19 and were not in hospital when the blood was drawn. ?incov_pbmc_subset gives the sources, their licences and every step from the public files to the object.

y <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "incov_pbmc_subset.rds",
    package = "exposomeSC"))
y
#> class: SingleCellExposomeExperiment 
#> dim: 15406 1032 
#> metadata(3): source plasma_metabolites metabolite_info
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(15406): A1BG A1BG-AS1 ... ZYX ZZEF1
#> rowData names(1): symbol
#> colnames(1032): INCOV039_AAGACCTAGGGTCTCC INCOV039_ACTGTCCGTGAGGCTA ...
#>   INCOV135_GGCGTGTGTACCGTAT INCOV135_GTATCTTAGAAACGCC
#> colData names(4): donor_id cell_type sample_id archive_cell
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(1): CITE
#> exposureData(43 samples x 16 exposures): ever_smoker, age, sex_male, cotinine, caffeine ...
#> sampleColumn: donor_id
table(y$cell_type)
#> 
#> Monocyte   T cell 
#>      602      430
as.data.frame(exposureInfo(y)[, c("exposure", "family", "source_name")])
#>                 exposure         family                      source_name
#> 1            ever_smoker  tobacco smoke                Cigarette Smoking
#> 2                    age    demographic                              Age
#> 3               sex_male    demographic                              Sex
#> 4               cotinine        tobacco                         cotinine
#> 5               caffeine       caffeine                         caffeine
#> 6           paraxanthine       caffeine                     paraxanthine
#> 7            theobromine       caffeine                      theobromine
#> 8                   pfos perfluoroalkyl  perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS)
#> 9                   pfoa perfluoroalkyl        perfluorooctanoate (PFOA)
#> 10 methylparaben_sulfate        paraben methyl-4-hydroxybenzoate sulfate
#> 11 propylparaben_sulfate        paraben propyl 4-hydroxybenzoate sulfate
#> 12 hydroxychlorothalonil      pesticide          4-hydroxychlorothalonil
#> 13      naphthol_sulfate    naphthalene               2-naphthol sulfate
#> 14     ethyl_glucuronide        alcohol                ethyl glucuronide

Compounds without a value

The plasma levels are relative abundances from untargeted mass spectrometry, scaled by the authors so that the median of a compound within a batch is 1. For some donors the table has no value of a compound:

colSums(is.na(exposureData(y)[, c("caffeine", "paraxanthine", "theobromine",
    "pfos", "pfoa", "saccharin")]))
#>     caffeine paraxanthine  theobromine         pfos         pfoa    saccharin 
#>            3            3            0            1            1           16

The table does not say why a value is missing. In such measurements the usual reason is that the compound was not detected, but it is not the only one, and the data can speak against it. Paraxanthine is the main metabolite of caffeine:

pair <- exposureData(y)[, c("caffeine", "paraxanthine")]
round(pair[!complete.cases(pair), ], 2)
#>          caffeine paraxanthine
#> INCOV039     9.82           NA
#> INCOV068     4.24           NA
#> INCOV081     2.87           NA
#> INCOV109       NA         0.04
#> INCOV116       NA         0.05
#> INCOV134       NA         0.27

The donors without a value of caffeine have little paraxanthine, which fits caffeine that was not detected. The donors without a value of paraxanthine have caffeine well above the median of their batch, which is 1; their paraxanthine is unlikely to have been below detection, so paraxanthine is left out of what follows.

exposure_impute_lod() replaces values below a limit of detection (LOD), by substitution, by regression on order statistics ("ros") or by multiple imputation ("multiple"). censored marks the values that were below the limit; a missing value that is not marked stays missing.

Three things are assumed here to show the function, and none is in the source. The section takes every missing value of the five compounds below to be a compound that was not detected. The table reports no limits of detection; the smallest value of a compound among all samples of the study, kept in exposureInfo(y)$lowest_reported, stands in for the limit, although the values were scaled batch by batch and one limit for all batches is itself an approximation. And "ros" takes the logarithms of the levels to be normally distributed.

compounds <- c("caffeine", "theobromine", "pfos", "pfoa", "saccharin")
reported <- exposureData(y)[, compounds]
info <- exposureInfo(y)
lowest <- setNames(info$lowest_reported, info$exposure)[compounds]
signif(lowest, 2)
#>    caffeine theobromine        pfos        pfoa   saccharin 
#>      0.0190      0.0016      0.0720      0.0650      0.0910
filled <- exposure_impute_lod(reported, lod = lowest, method = "ros",
    censored = is.na(reported))
#> caffeine: 3 below LOD, 0 missing, 40 detected
#> theobromine: 0 below LOD, 0 missing, 43 detected
#> pfos: 1 below LOD, 0 missing, 42 detected
#> pfoa: 1 below LOD, 0 missing, 42 detected
#> saccharin: 16 below LOD, 0 missing, 27 detected
attr(filled, "lod_summary")
#>      exposure n_detected n_censored n_missing method
#> 1    caffeine         40          3         0    ros
#> 2 theobromine         43          0         0   none
#> 3        pfos         42          1         0    ros
#> 4        pfoa         42          1         0    ros
#> 5   saccharin         27         16         0    ros
fill_over_limit <- function(compound) {
    gone <- is.na(reported[, compound])
    round(sort(filled[gone, compound]) / lowest[[compound]], 3)
}
fill_over_limit("caffeine")
#> INCOV109 INCOV116 INCOV134 
#>    0.999    0.999    0.999
fill_over_limit("saccharin")
#> INCOV039 INCOV042 INCOV057 INCOV058 INCOV078 INCOV081 INCOV088 INCOV094 
#>    0.047    0.100    0.153    0.210    0.271    0.337    0.408    0.485 
#> INCOV100 INCOV102 INCOV103 INCOV107 INCOV116 INCOV131 INCOV132 INCOV134 
#>    0.569    0.661    0.760    0.869    0.987    0.999    0.999    0.999

"ros" gives one filled-in value for each missing one. The fills follow the distribution fitted to the reported values and say nothing about which donor had the larger level, which suits a summary and not an association. With a limit as low as the one assumed here, the three fills of caffeine all lie just below it, and only saccharin, with 16 missing values, gets a spread of them. For an association analysis ?exposure_impute_lod advises method = "multiple", which returns several filled-in data sets to analyse one by one and combine; the sections below use the single "ros" fill all the same, to stay short.

The logarithms of the filled levels replace the reported levels in the object; exposureData<- checks that the donors still agree with the cells, and exposureInfo<- records what the values now are.

levels <- exposureData(y)
levels[, compounds] <- log2(filled)
exposureData(y) <- levels
round(head(exposureData(y)[, compounds], 3), 2)
#>          caffeine theobromine  pfos  pfoa saccharin
#> INCOV039     3.30       -0.19 -0.92 -0.78     -7.88
#> INCOV042    -0.03        0.67  1.35 -1.22     -6.79
#> INCOV056     2.66       -0.06 -1.06 -0.07      1.74
info$unit[match(compounds, info$exposure)] <-
    "log2 of the relative abundance, missing values filled in"
exposureInfo(y) <- info
unique(exposureInfo(y)$unit)
#> [1] "1 = current or former smoker, 0 = never smoker"          
#> [2] "years"                                                   
#> [3] "1 = male, 0 = female"                                    
#> [4] "relative abundance, median of a batch = 1"               
#> [5] "log2 of the relative abundance, missing values filled in"

Dose and response

run_dose_response() compares polynomial models of a gene’s pseudobulk expression on a continuous exposure within one cell type, and run_dose_response_gam() fits a smooth curve with mgcv. The dose here is the plasma level of caffeine, and the genes are 12 interferon-stimulated genes with counts in most donors, which serve as the outcome in the rest of this section because the donors had a viral infection.

interferon <- c("IFI6", "ISG15", "MX1", "IFITM3", "STAT1", "XAF1", "EPSTI1",
    "LY6E", "IRF7", "ISG20", "MX2", "EIF2AK2")
dose <- run_dose_response(y, exposure = "caffeine", celltype = "Monocyte",
    target_genes = interferon)
head(dose[order(dose$p_nonlinear), c("gene", "best_model", "linear_coef",
    "p_nonlinear", "n_donors")], 4)
#> DataFrame with 4 rows and 5 columns
#>          gene  best_model linear_coef p_nonlinear  n_donors
#>   <character> <character>   <numeric>   <numeric> <integer>
#> 1       ISG15   quadratic  -0.1056280    0.139063        43
#> 2      EPSTI1      linear  -0.1623649    0.369017        43
#> 3     EIF2AK2      linear  -0.0635761    0.373550        43
#> 4        IFI6      linear  -0.2664277    0.412985        43

best_model is the polynomial with the lowest AIC, and p_nonlinear an F test of the cubic against the linear model; it is not adjusted for the number of genes.

smooth <- run_dose_response_gam(y, exposure = "caffeine",
    celltype = "Monocyte", target_genes = interferon[1:4])
smooth[, c("gene", "edf", "p_smooth", "p_nonlinear", "R2_loocv_gam")]
#> DataFrame with 4 rows and 5 columns
#>          gene       edf  p_smooth p_nonlinear R2_loocv_gam
#>   <character> <numeric> <numeric>   <numeric>    <numeric>
#> 1        IFI6   1.00011 0.0385404   0.4335986   0.00947767
#> 2       ISG15   1.93161 0.1655689   0.0769601  -0.01951944
#> 3         MX1   1.00006 0.5223509   0.7782516  -0.07199001
#> 4      IFITM3   1.00002 0.0900116   0.4186522  -0.07171163

Mixtures

run_sc_mixture() scores each exposure by its quantile and regresses the pseudobulk expression of each target gene on the scores; it returns the sum of the coefficients for each gene and, in the metadata, the relative size of the coefficients of each exposure. It is a screen, without intervals or tests. run_mixture_qgcomp() fits quantile g-computation (Keil et al. 2020) with qgcomp to the mean expression of the target genes and returns an interval and a p-value for the effect of raising all exposures by one quantile.

mixture_of <- c("caffeine", "theobromine", "pfos", "pfoa")
mixture <- run_sc_mixture(y, exposures = mixture_of, celltype = "Monocyte",
    target_genes = interferon, covariates = c("age", "sex_male"))
head(mixture[order(-abs(mixture$mixture_effect)), ], 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 2 columns
#>          gene mixture_effect
#>   <character>      <numeric>
#> 1        IFI6      -0.987597
#> 2      EPSTI1      -0.635306
#> 3      IFITM3      -0.528017
round(metadata(mixture)$weights, 2)
#>    caffeine theobromine        pfos        pfoa 
#>        0.30        0.23        0.16        0.31
joint <- run_mixture_qgcomp(y, exposures = mixture_of, celltype = "Monocyte",
    target_genes = interferon, covariates = c("age", "sex_male"))
joint[, c("mixture_effect", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "mixture_pvalue",
    "n_donors")]
#> DataFrame with 1 row and 5 columns
#>   mixture_effect  ci_lower  ci_upper mixture_pvalue  n_donors
#>        <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>      <numeric> <integer>
#> 1      -0.328523  -1.02009   0.36304       0.341756        43

Genes and proteins

run_cell_coupling() is for data with surface proteins measured in the same cells, kept as an alternative experiment. Within each donor it computes the Spearman partial correlation between a gene and a protein across the cells of one cell type, given the RNA and protein library sizes; a meta-regression across the donors then asks whether this correlation differs with the exposure. It takes every gene with every protein; the rows of five genes with their own proteins are shown.

pairs <- data.frame(
    gene = c("HLA-DRA", "CD36", "ITGAM", "FCGR3A", "CD86"),
    protein = c("HLA-DR", "CD36-1", "CD11B", "CD16", "CD86-1")
)
coupling <- run_cell_coupling(y, genes = pairs$gene,
    proteins = pairs$protein, exposure = "ever_smoker", celltype = "Monocyte",
    min_cells = 14L)
#> [exposomeSC] Cell coupling: Monocyte, 5 genes x 5 proteins = 25 pairs, 2 confounders
#> [exposomeSC] 25 pairs tested for Monocyte
own <- paste(coupling$gene, coupling$protein) %in%
    paste(pairs$gene, pairs$protein)
coupling[own, c("gene", "protein", "n_donors", "mean_r", "beta1", "se1",
    "pval1")]
#> DataFrame with 5 rows and 7 columns
#>          gene     protein  n_donors    mean_r      beta1       se1     pval1
#>   <character> <character> <integer> <numeric>  <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>
#> 1     HLA-DRA      HLA-DR        43 0.2696685 0.32435086  0.130771 0.0173242
#> 2        CD36      CD36-1        43 0.1099379 0.11703345  0.127730 0.3648920
#> 3       ITGAM       CD11B        39 0.1128381 0.21469605  0.122741 0.0885514
#> 4      FCGR3A        CD16        39 0.3816497 0.10903979  0.131641 0.4128062
#> 5        CD86      CD86-1        39 0.0581079 0.00191838  0.119037 0.9872286

mean_r is the mean of the partial correlation over the donors, and beta1 the slope, across donors, of its Fisher z on the exposure. The default min_cells is 30 cells per donor; the data have 14 monocytes per donor, too few for an analysis that is meant to be read.

Related packages

exposomeSC adds a container for donor-level exposures and analyses that are specific to exposure studies; for the model fits themselves it calls other packages. The pseudobulk counts are summed by scrapper, and the models are those of edgeR, DESeq2 and limma with variancePartition. The packages below cover neighbouring ground.

  • muscat analyses differential states in multi-sample, multi-group single-cell data, with pseudobulk and mixed-model methods. run_sc_exwas() fits a pseudobulk model of the same kind for a donor-level exposure that is kept in the object.
  • dreamlet tests pseudobulk differential expression in complex study designs, with the mixed models of variancePartition. method = "voom_dream" calls variancePartition itself, without a random effect; it does not use dreamlet.
  • rexposome and omicRexposome hold exposome data and associate them with bulk omic data. as_scee() takes the exposures of an ExposomeSet of rexposome into the container.
  • speckle, crumblr and sccomp test differences in the composition of cell types, as run_exposure_composition() does; its help page describes how it differs from each.

A study whose question is a comparison of groups of samples, without exposure measurements to keep with the cells, is served by the first two packages directly.
